channel.title: Athene Softworks Blog
channel.description: Notes on security and AI from the team behind Agamemnon and Synapse.

item.title: Public Wi-Fi in 2026: what's actually risky, and what isn't
item.description: HTTPS has made café Wi-Fi far safer than the old warnings suggest. But a few real risks remain: fake hotspots, captive portals and the DNS lookups that still reveal where you go. Here's what to do about each.

item.title: Infostealers: the malware that wants your logins, not your files
item.description: The most common malware today doesn't lock or wreck your computer. It quietly copies your passwords, cookies and wallets, then disappears. Here's how it works and how to stop it.

item.title: How to host your own AI model, for free or close to it
item.description: From a model on your laptop to a private API your phone and friends can use. Four practical ways to host an open model, what each costs, and the security mistake almost everyone makes.

item.title: Running AI on your own computer vs. in the cloud
item.description: Local models keep everything private and work offline. Cloud models are smarter and faster. What your hardware can actually run, and how to pick for each job.

item.title: ClickFix: when a web page asks you to paste a command
item.description: A fake CAPTCHA tells you to press a few keys to prove you're human. Those keys run malware. Here's how the trick works on Windows and Mac, and the one rule that beats it.

item.title: Free cloud AI: getting API keys from Google, Groq and OpenRouter
item.description: You don't need a subscription to use powerful cloud models. Where to get free API keys, what the limits look like, what happens to your data, and how to keep a key from leaking.

item.title: How antivirus actually finds malware: fingerprints, rules and behaviour
item.description: A look inside a modern antivirus engine: why a single hash catches millions of copies, what YARA rules are, and why watching behaviour is what stops brand-new threats.

item.title: BadUSB: when a USB stick pretends to be a keyboard
item.description: Some USB devices aren't drives at all. Plugged in, they announce themselves as a keyboard and type commands faster than you can blink. How these attacks work and how to protect yourself.

item.title: Viruses, worms, trojans and ransomware: a plain-language guide
item.description: "Virus" has become the word for every kind of malware, but the differences matter: they decide how something spreads and how you protect yourself. A short field guide.

item.title: Backups that survive ransomware: the 3-2-1 rule, made simple
item.description: A backup that's always plugged in can be encrypted along with everything else. How to set up backups on a Mac or PC that ransomware, a stolen laptop or a spilled coffee can't take away.

item.title: Prompt injection: how a web page can hijack your AI assistant
item.description: When an AI can browse, read your files or run commands, any text it reads becomes a possible instruction. What prompt injection is, why nobody has fully solved it, and how to use AI agents safely anyway.

item.title: Cracked software is the stealers' favourite delivery van
item.description: Free Photoshop, a game cheat, a 'portable' Office: the most common way infostealers reach home computers is a download people chose themselves. How the trap is set and how to get software safely.

item.title: How much memory do you need to run AI locally?
item.description: 8 GB, 16 GB, 32 GB or more: what each amount of RAM or VRAM actually lets you run, why Apple Silicon Macs punch above their weight, and a quick formula to check any model before you download it.

item.title: Passkeys explained: the login that can't be phished
item.description: Passkeys replace passwords with a key that lives on your phone or computer. What they are, why a fake site can't steal them, and how to switch your most important accounts in ten minutes.

item.title: Q4_K_M, Q8_0, FP16: model quantization in plain words
item.description: Download a local AI model and you're faced with a list of cryptic file names. What quantization is, how much quality each level really costs, and which file to pick for your computer.

item.title: How to spot a phishing message before you click
item.description: Phishing emails and texts no longer have spelling mistakes. Here are the signs that still give them away, and a simple habit that protects you even when a fake looks perfect.
